header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking

related.why: The examination that follows this history
Tumour types, markers and spread in more depth

brief.scenario: Mr Owen Penhale, 32, has been referred by his GP with a lump in his right testicle.
brief.task: Take a focused history. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to summarise, then asked about investigation and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: A painless lump in the body of the testis is cancer until proven otherwise. Ask risk factors, spread and fertility.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Accepting a minor knock as the cause of the lump.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Is the lump part of the testicle itself, or separate from it?"

grid.label: Opening and sensitivity
grid.fail: Asks intimate questions abruptly with no explanation.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, open question; explains he'll ask some personal questions.
grid.high: Normalises embarrassment and checks whether he'd like a chaperone for the examination later.

grid.label: The lump and alternatives
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about pain, size change or infective symptoms.
grid.pass: Onset, how noticed, size change, pain or heaviness, trauma; urinary symptoms, discharge, fever and sexual risk.
grid.high: Asks whether the lump is in the testis or separate from it, and treats a recent knock as how it was noticed, not the cause.

grid.label: Risk factors
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about undescended testis or family history.
grid.pass: Undescended testis or orchidopexy, previous testicular cancer, father or brother with testicular cancer, fertility problems.
grid.high: Links cryptorchidism and a small testis to contralateral risk, to raise at the treatment discussion.

grid.label: Symptoms of spread
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about back pain or chest symptoms.
grid.pass: Asks back or abdominal pain, cough, breathlessness, haemoptysis, weight loss, neck lump.
grid.high: Asks about breast swelling or tenderness (hCG) and explains back pain can come from para-aortic nodes.

grid.label: Fertility and concerns
grid.fail: Doesn't explore his worries or plans for children.
grid.pass: Asks what he is worried about and about plans for children.
grid.high: Raises sperm banking before any treatment and offers a prosthesis if the testis is removed.

grid.label: Summary at the signal
grid.fail: Presents it as a probable cyst or an injury.
grid.pass: Summarises a painless intratesticular lump over two months with relevant risk factors and states suspected testicular cancer.
grid.high: Leads with the lump's features and risk factors, then the negatives for spread and infection.

grid.label: Investigation
grid.fail: Plans no ultrasound, or omits tumour markers before surgery.
grid.pass: Urgent bilateral scrotal ultrasound; AFP, hCG and LDH before orchidectomy; contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis if cancer.
grid.high: Repeats markers after orchidectomy; knows a significant AFP rise implies a non-seminomatous component.

grid.label: Definitive management
grid.fail: Plans a scrotal biopsy or scrotal orchidectomy.
grid.pass: Radical inguinal orchidectomy with the cord divided at the internal ring; urology cancer MDT.
grid.high: Explains why the scrotum isn't opened; offers contralateral biopsy discussion if high risk (volume under 12 mL, cryptorchidism).

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: You've got a lump down below? Did you hurt it?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Mr Penhale, 32, knocked his testicle playing football and has a lump, probably a haematoma or a cyst.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you investigate and manage?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A scan in a few weeks if it hasn't gone. If it looks suspicious, a scrotal biopsy.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the urology trainees. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? Tell me what you noticed. I'll need to ask some personal questions; is that OK?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: When did you notice it? Has it grown? Any pain or heaviness? Any injury? Any burning passing urine, discharge or fever?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Were your testicles both down as a baby, or did you need an operation? Has anyone in the family had testicular cancer? Any problems with fertility?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Any back or tummy pain, cough, breathlessness or coughing blood? Any weight loss or lumps in your neck?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What's worrying you most? Do you have or want children?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Penhale, 32, with a two-month painless, enlarging right testicular lump. He had a right orchidopexy as a child. No symptoms of spread or infection. I suspect testicular cancer.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you investigate and manage?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urgent scrotal ultrasound of both testes; AFP, hCG and LDH before surgery. If it's a tumour, radical inguinal orchidectomy, contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, and MDT discussion.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the urology trainees. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? Lots of men find this awkward; I ask everyone these questions. I'll also offer a chaperone when I examine you.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Does the lump feel part of the testicle, or separate above or behind it? You mentioned a knock: was the lump there before?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Your right testicle was brought down as a child; that raises the risk, and we'd think about the other side too.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any breast swelling or tenderness? Back pain can come from glands at the back of the tummy, so I ask about that too.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Before any treatment, we can store sperm. If a testicle is removed, you can have a prosthesis.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Mr Penhale, 32: two months of a painless, enlarging lump within the right testis, noticed after a minor knock. Right orchidopexy aged 4. No back pain, chest or breast symptoms, weight loss or infective features. Wants children. Suspected right testicular germ cell tumour.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you investigate and manage?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Urgent bilateral scrotal ultrasound; AFP, hCG and LDH before orchidectomy and repeated after. A significant AFP rise means a non-seminomatous component. Sperm banking, then radical inguinal orchidectomy dividing the cord at the internal ring; we avoid the scrotum so lymphatic spread stays predictable. Contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging, MDT, and a discussion about biopsy of the left testis if it's under 12 mL.

failures.move: Planning scrotal biopsy or a scrotal approach.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: breaches the scrotum, altering lymphatic spread and risking local recurrence.
Delays diagnosis of a tumour that the knock only drew attention to.

failures.move: Delaying ultrasound or skipping pre-operative markers.
failures.consequence: Loses the baseline needed for staging, prognosis and follow-up.
He loses the chance to bank sperm before orchidectomy or chemotherapy.

recovery.line: Can I go back to one thing: were both testicles down when you were a child?

recovery.when: He asks directly if it's cancer
recovery.line: It could be, and I'd rather check quickly. Testicular cancer is usually very treatable, and the scan today is the first step.

knowledge.fact: Bilateral high-frequency testicular ultrasound for all suspected cancer; AFP, hCG and LDH before orchidectomy and repeated after.
Radical inguinal orchidectomy with cord division at the internal ring; avoid a scrotal approach. Offer a prosthesis.
Contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging. Discuss sperm banking with all men before treatment.
High risk of contralateral germ cell neoplasia: testicular volume under 12 mL and/or cryptorchidism history.
Consider suspected cancer referral for non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis.
Testicular lymph drains to para-aortic nodes.

recall.think: Germ cell tumour; metastases to para-aortic nodes and lungs.
recall.say: "A painless intratesticular lump is cancer until proven otherwise."

numbers.meaning: contralateral testis smaller than this: high risk, discuss biopsy

recall.trap: A minor knock that explains the lump.
recall.finish: Sperm banking, radical inguinal orchidectomy, CT staging, MDT.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9-minute stations with 1 minute's reading; introduce yourself and confirm identity

sources.name: European Association of Urology: Guidelines on Testicular Cancer
sources.supports: Bilateral testicular ultrasound in all suspected cases; AFP, hCG and LDH before and after orchidectomy; contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis; inguinal orchidectomy with cord division at internal ring, avoid scrotal approach; offer prosthesis; discuss sperm banking; contralateral biopsy for high risk (volume under 12 mL, cryptorchidism); significant AFP elevation in seminoma suggests NSGCT component

sources.name: NICE NG12: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral
sources.supports: 1.6.7: consider suspected cancer pathway referral for non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis

sources.name: Gray's Anatomy for Students (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell)
sources.supports: Lymphatic drainage of the testis to para-aortic nodes; scrotal skin to superficial inguinal nodes

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Mr Penhale. I'll stop you at 6 minutes to summarise.
partner.actorBrief: You are Owen Penhale, 32, a PE teacher, married, no children yet. Opening line: "I've noticed a lump in my right testicle. It doesn't hurt. I'm worried." Embarrassed; brief answers until put at ease. You think a football knock caused it; mention the knock early. Hidden fear: not being able to have children; say so only if asked about worries or children. Volunteer nothing else; give facts only when asked (see reveals).

reveals.finding: "We've just started trying for a baby. Will this stop that?"
Noticed two months ago in the shower after a football knock; slowly bigger; dull heaviness, no pain.

reveals.trigger: Asks whether it's part of the testicle
reveals.finding: "It's in the testicle itself, hard, near the front."

reveals.trigger: Asks urinary, discharge, fever, sexual risk

reveals.finding: "I had an operation on the right side when I was 4 to bring it down."
No family history. No known fertility problems; trying for six months.

reveals.trigger: Asks back pain, chest, breast, weight, neck

reveals.finding: Say: "Please stop there and summarise your history."

push.question: How would you investigate?
push.expect: Urgent bilateral scrotal ultrasound; AFP, hCG, LDH before surgery; CT chest, abdomen and pelvis if cancer.

push.question: The ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular mass. What next?
push.expect: Sperm banking, radical inguinal orchidectomy, prosthesis offered, MDT.

push.question: Why not remove it through the scrotum?
push.expect: Scrotal violation alters lymphatic drainage and risks local recurrence.

curveballs.prompt: "The AFP is raised but the orchidectomy histology shows pure seminoma."
curveballs.safeAnswer: A significant AFP rise implies a non-seminomatous component; manage as non-seminoma with the MDT.

curveballs.prompt: "Can I just wait and see if it goes down?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: a solid lump in the testis needs prompt diagnosis; earlier treatment is simpler and more effective.

curveballs.prompt: "Will I be able to have children?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Many men do with one testis; we'll offer sperm storage before treatment to protect that.
